newsitem.title: USA: GE opens contract talks with unions.
newsitem.headline: GE opens contract talks with unions.

text.p: General Electric Co opened contract negotiations Wednesday in New York City with the AFL-CIO Coordination Bargaining Committee (CBC), which represents thousands of GE workers whose three-year contracts expire June 29.

While Wall Street analysts say that it is too early to predict whether a strike will occur, they say a strike would have little impact on GE, which is generally considered well-managed and financially strong.

But with contract expirations a month away, management and labor don't even publicly agree on how many workers are covered by the talks. The unions say negotiations will affect 46,000 GE workers in 14 unions, while GE says the contracts cover 37,800 workers in a dozen unions.
Both sides, however, agree that the largest union involved is the International Union of Electricians, Electrical, Salaried, Machine and Furniture Workers (IUE), which has 22,000 workers at GE.

The unions said they are expecting "difficult negotiations." Uppermost in the minds of the CBC are not wages or salaries, but issues of job security. A CBC spokeswoman said that since 1986, union ranks at GE have fallen by half as a result of outsourcing, downsizing and the movement of jobs overseas.

"Our position is that we think the company should assure everybody's job for the life of the agreement," said Ed Fire, president of IUE. "They should also agree to a plant closing moratorium for the length of the agreement."
Fire said that the unions would consider early retirement options if the terms were good enough and would back certain productivity improvements.

GE chief negotiator Dennis Rochleau said in a statement that "from the company's perspective, every proposal we discuss in these negotiations must be considered against how it affects the future competitiveness of GE's diverse global business."
Analysts, however, say that in the event of a strike, the effect on shareholders should not be great.
"Any disruption by a strike is considered non-recurring and the stock market tends to overlook it," said Marvin Roffman of Roffman Miller Associates.
